title: Public Oil, Private Markets: Strategic Petroleum Reserve Exchanges and the Case for Public-Benefit Conditions
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: Public Oil, Private Markets: Strategic Petroleum Reserve Exchanges and the Case for Public-Benefit Conditions
detail.abstract: The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) was created after the oil shocks of the 1970s as a national-security asset intended to protect the country against severe supply disruptions. Recent large-scale SPR releases and exchanges, including emergency actions tied to Middle East supply instability, raise governance questions that are often overlooked: when publicly owned emergency oil is released into private and global markets, what public-benefit conditions should attach, and how low can the reserve be drawn before additional democratic authorization is required? Current policy discussion often focuses on whether released barrels are later replaced, sometimes with additional premium barrels. That accounting approach is incomplete. A barrel returned next year does not eliminate the public risk created when the reserve is depleted during an active crisis. Nor does repayment alone ensure that the original release benefited domestic consumers rather than refiners, traders, exporters, or global buyers. This paper argues that SPR releases and exchanges should be evaluated not only by inventory replacement, but also by transparency, domestic-consumer benefit, anti-arbitrage safeguards, emergency-readiness thresholds, and public accountability. It proposes a public-benefit framework requiring disclosure of recipient firms, contract terms, resale or export restrictions, repayment schedules, enforcement provisions, windfall-profit clawbacks, and a statutory stop-loss rule requiring explicit congressional authorization below a defined strategic floor. The SPR is a public asset. Emergency use of that asset should require measurable public return and a clear limit on executive depletion.

title: From Neoclassical to Computative Labor: Foundations for a Testable Theory of Reputation Governance in the Agent Economy
affiliations: University of St. Thomas - School of Law (Minnesota)

detail.title: From Neoclassical to Computative Labor: Foundations for a Testable Theory of Reputation Governance in the Agent Economy
detail.abstract: Artificial agents are becoming economic actors, performing open-ended cognitive work at a marginal cost that approaches zero. Neoclassical economics, built on scarce human labor allocated by price, does not describe this regime. This paper sets out the foundations of an alternative and argues that the alternative is empirically testable now. We distinguish the neoclassical labor force (NCLF) and neoclassical labor market (NCLM) from their computative counterparts, the computative labor force (CELF) and computative labor market (CELM), in which the binding coordination constraint is accumulated reputation rather than scarcity-driven price. From a synthesis of Arrow's impossibility theorem, the Folk Theorems of repeated games, and incomplete-contract theory, we restate a foundational result: any fixed governance rule set is eventually dominated, so coordination among autonomous agents requires institutions that govern their own evolution, with reputation as the operative signal. We then advance the methodological claim that motivates the paper. The distinction between neoclassical and computative labor is studiable today, because capable agents, on-chain coordination substrates, and reputation primitives already exist, and the competing predictions of the two accounts are falsifiable in controlled multi-agent settings. We situate the argument within a sixpaper research arc that substantiates these foundations, and we state the propositions the arc evaluates. The governance mechanism and the empirical results are developed elsewhere in the arc and are deliberately outside the scope of this paper.

detail.abstract: Falls from height have been the leading cause of workplace fatalities in Great Britain in almost every year since 2001. In the 2024/25 reporting period, 35 workers died as a result of such fallsover a quarter of all worker deaths that year. The construction sector bears a disproportionate share, and within construction, pitched roof maintenance is among the highest-risk activities. This paper introduces the Access-Cost Trapa structural dynamic in the residential roof cleaning market where the dominant cost of safe access (scaffolding) and the dominant cost of fall prevention are the same line item, creating a market-level incentive for safety underinvestment that enforcement alone cannot resolve. Three testable propositions are derived and evaluated against HSE prosecution data, industry pricing evidence, and the academic literature on automation and occupational safety. The paper situates this problem within established occupational safety theory-Heinrich's accident triangle, Reason's Swiss Cheese model, and the hierarchy of controlsand extends it to argue that autonomous drone-robot systems represent a qualitatively different intervention class: they address the trap at its root by eliminating the need for human height exposure entirely, rather than adding further management layers above it. Drawing on peer-reviewed evidence from comparable autonomous systems (Kishor et al., Scientific Reports, 2025; De Simone et al., 2025, working paper) and the Law Commission's May 2026 final report on aviation autonomy, the paper concludes with the Autonomous Roof Maintenance Adoption Framework (ARMAF)a three-pillar policy roadmap with specific recommendations directed at the HSE, the CAA, and the NFRC.

title: Data Element Utilization and Innovation–Industrial Chain Integration in Manufacturing Firms: A Dynamic Capabilities Perspective
affiliations: Chongqing Normal University and Chongqing Normal University

detail.title: Data Element Utilization and Innovation–Industrial Chain Integration in Manufacturing Firms: A Dynamic Capabilities Perspective
detail.abstract: Digital transformation has intensified the need for manufacturing firms to connect technological innovation with industrial application. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory, this study conceptualizes data element utilization as a capability enabling resource that helps firms sense technological opportunities, seize transformation initiatives, and reconfigure innovation and industrial resources. Using an unbalanced panel of Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2011 to 2023, we examine the effect of data element utilization on the breadth and depth of innovation–industrial chain integration. Data element utilization is measured from the perspective of corporate data asset value realization, while innovation–industrial chain integration is constructed using joint patent application data. The results show that data element utilization significantly enhances both the breadth and depth of innovation–industrial chain integration, and the findings remain robust across a series of additional tests. Mechanism analyses reveal three pathways: smart manufacturing investment, innovation quality improvement, and innovation boundary expansion. Smart manufacturing investment and innovation quality improvement exhibit one-period lagged effects, suggesting that the resource allocation and knowledge accumulation enabled by data elements require time to materialize. By contrast, innovation boundary expansion shows an immediate effect, indicating that data elements can rapidly reduce information frictions and broaden firms’ technological search scope. Further analyses show that market attention and platform ecosystem embeddedness strengthen the positive effect of data element utilization on innovation–industrial chain integration. This study extends research on innovation–industrial chain integration by highlighting the role of data elements and provides firm-level evidence on how data element utilization enables high-quality manufacturing development through dynamic capability mechanisms.

title: A Reliability-Aware PHM Inference Framework for Weakly Labeled Non-Stationary Stamping Press Vibration Under Distribution Shift
affiliations: National Taiwan University of Science and Technology

detail.title: A Reliability-Aware PHM Inference Framework for Weakly Labeled Non-Stationary Stamping Press Vibration Under Distribution Shift
detail.abstract: Stamping presses operate under repetitive impacts and high dynamic loads, making raw structural vibration strongly non-stationary and difficult to use for reliable operating-state inference in real factories. In practice, stamping-press vibration is logged as short fixed-duration segments, for example 15 seconds, under a single nominal speed–load operating recipe, so labels are naturally defined at the file level, while individual window-level predictions within a segment can be highly noisy due to transient impacts and within-interval variability. This work proposes a reliability-aware PHM inference framework for weakly labeled non-stationary stamping press vibration under distribution shift, formulated as file-level multi-class operating-state classification using raw triaxial accelerometer data and a compact LSTM operating on overlapping sliding windows. A reliability-aware inference layer with class-specific confidence gating, temporal smoothing, and file-level majority voting converts noisy window streams into stable operating-state labels that are directly usable in manufacturing execution and predictive maintenance workflows. Window-level predictions are further treated as a reliability channel: confidence-filtered accuracy, retained-window coverage, and class-wise confusion patterns are monitored as early-warning indicators of distribution shift and used to trigger replay-based continual updates before file-level performance degrades. To perform these updates, we introduce ReACT (Reliability-Aware Continued Training), which adapts class-dependent loss weights and per-class confidence thresholds on validation data and selects checkpoints by confidence-filtered validation accuracy. Experiments on training, validation, and independent drift-test datasets from a real stamping line show that, although all-window accuracy remains modest, the confidence-gated subset achieves high reliability while using only a small fraction of windows, and file-level accuracy, the deployment target, reaches 100\% on validation and test data. These results demonstrate that combining window-level reliability monitoring with confidence-aware selection, aggregation, and ReACT-based continual training can turn noisy, weakly labeled, non-stationary stamping press vibration into stable, drift-sensitive PHM decisions suitable for resource-constrained edge devices.

title: Advancements in Trajectory Prediction for Data-Driven Situational Awareness: Survey of Current Literature

detail.abstract: The increasing complexity of modern transportation networks has always pushed the need for improved traffic management and situational awareness. At the center of these goals is an understanding or model of the relationships between the individual components and the dynamic environment in which they operate. Maritime and aviation controls must deal with an enormous volume of traffic operating under changing weather conditions, a variety of international traffic rules and customs, different mission goals of different platform types, and the usual unpredictability of human behavior. Early statistical methods provided initial insights into the character and behavior of these complex environments. Those early successes then encouraged industrial efforts to automatically collect real-time data from on-board radio broadcasts. The Automatic Identification System (AIS) evolved for international shipping and was then followed by Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) capabilities for aviation. The resulting surge of real-time location data enabled the use of machine learning and deep learning techniques to significantly improve trajectory prediction. These predictions, in turn, have enhanced routing optimization, collision avoidance, anomaly detection, and emergency response management. This paper presents a critical review of the evolution of data-driven research in maritime and aviation traffic analysis. It covers key developments and points out several ongoing challenges in the designing of robust and generalizable models that help capture the complexity of this evergrowing traffic environment.

title: The Winner's Bliss in Common-value Auctions under Horizontal Differentiation
affiliations: University of California, Irvine, Carnegie Mellon University - David A. Tepper School of Business, Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics, Students and California Institute of Technology (Caltech)

detail.title: The Winner's Bliss in Common-value Auctions under Horizontal Differentiation
detail.abstract: We study common-value auctions in which bidders have horizontally differentiated preferences. In a specific two-bidder parameterization, winning conveys good news about the object's value to the winner, a phenomenon we call the "winner's bliss," in contrast to the conventional winner's curse. Additional implications also differ from the conventional analysis. When bidder's preferences are horizontally differentiated, seller revenue is decreasing in information disclosure, and advantageous selection sustains bilateral trade under asymmetric information.

title: The Four Layers of AI Governance An Architecture for Governing the Agent Economy

detail.title: The Four Layers of AI Governance An Architecture for Governing the Agent Economy
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence shifts from a tool that people operate to a workforce of autonomous agents that hold goals, take actions, and interact over time, the central problem of AI safety shifts with it-from the alignment of any individual model to the governance of agent collectives. This paper argues that the agent economy requires a governance stack analogous to the protocol stack of the internet, and proposes a four-layer architecture for it. The model layer concerns the capability, alignment, and judgment of the individual agent. The trust layer concerns bilateral, one-on-one relationships and the verification, reputation, and transaction-cost infrastructure that make agent-to-agent cooperation possible. The coordination layer concerns teams of agents and the organizational design needed to prevent redundancy, error cascades, and cross-purpose work within and between them. The institutional layer concerns the markets, rules, and norms governing the entire population of agents, where individually rational behavior can still produce collective failure. For each layer we identify the distinctive failure mode, the human institutions that historically addressed the analogous problem, and the open research and infrastructure agenda for rebuilding those institutions natively for software. We contend that the next frontier of value and safety in AI lies not in more capable agents, but in the institutions that let many of them act together without failing all at once.

title: The Great Methodological Regress: Restoring Falsifiability in Economic Science
affiliations: Zhejiang Guangsha Vocational and Technical University of Construction and Australian National University (ANU) - Crawford School of Public Policy

detail.title: The Great Methodological Regress: Restoring Falsifiability in Economic Science

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Modern economics is widely perceived as methodologically sophisticated, yet increasingly fragmented between abstract theory and empirical practice. This paper diagnoses this condition as a "Great Methodological Regress," characterized by a retreat from falsifiability as the core scientific standard. Drawing on Popperian philosophy of science and the methodological insights of Friedman (1953) and Cheung (2001), we develop a deductive framework for causal inference that distinguishes between reality-based constraints (x-type assumptions) and auxiliary simplifications (t-type assumptions). This distinction provides a clear criterion for assessing whether economic theories generate testable predictions or merely internal consistency. Applying this framework, we conduct a systematic audit of mainstream economics across theoretical, empirical, and experimental domains. We demonstrate that dominant approaches-from growth theory and DSGE modeling to quasi-experimental econometrics-frequently generate internally coherent or statistically credible results without delivering falsifiable causal explanations. These methods often rely on unobservable constructs (e.g., total factor productivity residuals, calibrated parameters, psychological biases) or statistical conveniences (e.g., weak instruments, parallel trends assumptions) that immunize theories against empirical refutation. In contrast, we reexamine the methodological exemplars of the Permanent Income Hypothesis by Friedman (1957), the Theory of Share Tenancy by Cheung (1969), and the transaction cost framework by Ding and Zhou (2021). These works illustrate a rigorous two-stage methodology: first deriving falsifiable predictions from clearly specified constraints, then designing empirical strategies that directly confront these predictions with observable data. The paper concludes by offering an operational standard-a "two-stage sieve" of falsifiable theory and theory-guided evidence-for restoring causal credibility and cumulative progress in economics.

title: 'Impact of Digital Marketing Techniques in the UAE Real Estate Market: A Mediation Model Examining the Effects on Business Outcome'

detail.title: 'Impact of Digital Marketing Techniques in the UAE Real Estate Market: A Mediation Model Examining the Effects on Business Outcome'

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is not personal or financial relationship with any other person or persons or organizations with respect to this study and for the publication of this article

detail.abstract: The UAE real estate businesses lack empirical clarity regarding the actual effectiveness of digital marketing strategies on business performance outcomes, such as sales revenue growth, customer acquisition, customer retention, and market share. While digital marketing investments in the UAE have grown at double-digit annual rates, many firms continue to report uncertainty in measuring return on investment (ROI) and difficulty in linking digital marketing activities to tangible performance indicators. This study analyzed the concepts, mechanisms, and evidence around four core digital marketing levers: Search Engine Optimization (SEO), Social Media Marketing (SMM), Email Marketing (EMM), and Content Marketing (CTM); and two behavioral outcomes that mediate those levers into firm performance, namely, Customer Engagement (CET) and Customer Satisfaction (CSN). It then considered the firm-level Business Outcomes (BO), such as, sales revenue growth, market share, brand loyalty, and customer retention. The study employed a stratified random sampling technique to ensure representative and diverse participation across various segments within the UAE real estate business sector. A sample size of 330 was selected. The conceptual framework developed for the study was examined by multivariate mediation analysis (Hayes’ Model 6). It was found that Search Engine Optimization technique is the most powerful digital marketing tool for enhancing customer satisfaction, and business outcome in UAE real estate business sector. SEO techniques significantly enhance the visibility and discoverability of real estate websites in the UAE; the use of relevant keywords and optimized content boosts organic traffic for real estate companies in the UAE market; implementing local SEO practices effectively targets and engages relevant audiences seeking property related information in the UAE, and regular updating and optimizing website content positively impacts search engine ranking for real estate businesses in the UAE.

title: Produce or Delegate? A Transaction-cost Theory of Vertical Integration: An Old Problem in the Age of AI

detail.abstract: This paper argues that recent differences between ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and other AI platforms reflect an old problem of economic organization rather than a purely technological divergence. The problem is whether the owner of a core asset should organize an adjacent commercial layer through specialization or vertical integration. Specialization and vertical integration are alternative ways of organizing that adjacent layer. The choice depends on the comparison between external transaction costs and internal management costs. External transaction costs include the costs of searching for capable outside actors, negotiating the relevant terms, and enforcing contractual performance. Internal management costs include the costs of supervising, coordinating, pricing, incentivizing, and organizing the activity within the firm. In the empirical cases examined below, this comparison often turns on whether outside performance can be enforced at acceptable cost. When outside performance is costly to enforce, vertical integration or strong control is more likely; when it can be enforced at acceptable cost, specialization becomes more feasible. The paper examines this tradeoff through comparative evidence from luxury and beauty groups, restaurants, franchising, logistics, contract manufacturing, complex system integration, and AI applications. Core luxury retail, fresh-prep food service, JD logistics, ASML system integration, and AI coding workflows illustrate cases in which outside performance is difficult to enforce because rent depends on service quality, outlet execution, fulfillment reliability, system integration, or workflow feedback. Beauty and eyewear licensing, standardized franchising, marketplace logistics, Nike and adidas contract manufacturing, and dispersed AI vertical applications illustrate cases in which outside performance can be enforced at acceptable cost because the relevant routines or interfaces are sufficiently standardized. In these cases, outside actors can perform the layer without destroying the rent attached to the core asset. In AI, this framework helps explain why coding workflows are attractive candidates for internalization or platform control, while dispersed vertical applications are more likely to be delegated to downstream firms, developers, cloud providers, and system integrators.

title: The Iterative Expression Doctrine

detail.title: The Iterative Expression Doctrine
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces and formally defines the Iterative Expression Doctrine: the principle that a person's
identity cannot be reduced to a single captured moment of expression. Identity is the integral of all outputs
across all time and all contexts — not a static data point frozen by an algorithm, a police encounter, or a
deleted social media post. Systems currently compress humans into low-context snapshots, and that
compression has measurable governance effects. The doctrine establishes six foundational observations, an
identity posture formula, a boundary condition that resolves the infinite deferral problem, and the Builder's
Grid — the two-part framework pairing this doctrine with the Token Zero Doctrine as a complete user-side
governance architecture. Five AI platforms stress-tested the doctrine across two days. Version 0.4
incorporates the legal rebuttal from Manus AI (ST-008): the affirmative-versus-defensive rights gap is
reframed as procedural due process; a Safe Harbor standard for AI-assisted expression is introduced; and the
execution checkpoint is defined with legal precision by domain. Godwin v. Godwin [2026] EWHC 923 (Ch) is
addressed directly.

title: Travel as Production: Endogenous in-trip Output, Scheduling, and the Bottleneck

detail.title: Travel as Production: Endogenous in-trip Output, Scheduling, and the Bottleneck

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Singapore National Research Foundation under its Campus for Research Excellence and Technological Enterprise (CREATE) programme.

detail.abstract: Automation, ride-hailing, and other passive services make travel time partly usable for work or rest. Transport choice then depends on what travellers can produce while moving, not only on money and clock time. I model travel as production. The final commodity is scheduled activity access, trips are intermediate inputs, and modes, routes, departure times, and vehicle technologies are production plans. Three results follow. First, the value of travel time is endogenous to within-trip work and rest. Active time costs the resource value of time plus effort; passive time costs that value net of reclaimed output. Under additive in-trip outputs, the model also yields a constant-returns implicit-price rule as a special case. Second, putting the production technology into a Vickrey/Arnott-de Palma-Lindsey bottleneck separates welfare and pricing effects. Productive in-vehicle time lengthens the physical queue but leaves money-metric generalised cost and the fine toll unchanged in the pure point bottleneck. This neutrality applies only to money-metric traveller cost, before spillback, vehicle-hour, energy, emissions, crash-exposure, and curb-space externalities are priced. Productive early arrival flattens the peak; lower free-flow travel cost under elastic demand induces trips and raises the optimal toll. Third, the production structure imposes falsifiable restrictions relative to generic random-utility and discrete-continuous models. Stylised simulations illustrate the results.

title: Towards Human-Centered AI Ecosystems: Examining the Health Implications of Robot Adoption for Workers
affiliations: Anhui University

detail.title: Towards Human-Centered AI Ecosystems: Examining the Health Implications of Robot Adoption for Workers
detail.abstract: Industrial robot adoption is transforming labor markets by reshaping skill requirements, employee roles, and overall workplace dynamics. While robotics-driven automation has been linked to productivity gains, its broader implications for worker wellbeing remain underexplored. Drawing on evidence from China, this study investigates the health effects of increased exposure to industrial robots within the framework of human-centered AI ecosystems. We find robust and persistent evidence that higher robot exposure significantly reduces the likelihood of workers remaining healthy, with a 10 percent increase in exposure associated with a 4.53 percent decline in self-reported health. The negative impact is primarily driven by two mechanisms: intensified labor demands and reduced income, disproportionately affecting low-skilled workers. Beyond physical strain, robot adoption also exacerbates mental health issues, with adverse effects reinforced through unhealthy coping behaviors among vulnerable groups. These findings highlight the socio-technical trade-offs of robotization and underline the need to design responsible AI ecosystems that safeguard worker health and promote inclusive wellbeing alongside technological progress.

title: Holding the Thread: AI-ALI and the Need for Personal Continuity in Long Human-AI Collaboration

detail.title: Holding the Thread: AI-ALI and the Need for Personal Continuity in Long Human-AI Collaboration

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes a practical partner in writing, research, design, education, media production, and cultural or spiritual documentation, a recurring problem is becoming visible: long AI conversations become heavy. They slow down, lose navigability, become difficult to transfer, or require the user to begin again in a new thread, device, or platform. This is not only a usability inconvenience. It reveals a deeper design gap in contemporary human-AI interaction: many systems are built to respond well to individual prompts, but they are less prepared to support long, cumulative, user-directed work. This paper proposes AI-ALI - an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Layer of Interpretation and Continuity - as a conceptual framework for preserving project continuity across sessions, platforms, and tools. AI-ALI is not presented as a finished technical system. It is proposed as a human-centered continuity layer that maintains active project state: decisions, terminology, corrections, structure, style, context, pending work, and transfer summaries. The paper argues that continuity must be personal rather than generic: even more powerful AI models remain limited when they operate without the user's singular distinctions, cultural context, project-specific rules, and governing corrections. AI-ALI should therefore be shaped by the individual user and governed by the user's own needs, language, workflows, corrections, and meaning-making. The framework contributes to discussions of human-centered AI, personal knowledge management, AI memory, digital authorship, and trustworthy AI assistance by distinguishing chat history from project state, memory from accountable continuity, and model capacity from personally faithful continuity.

title: CausalPrime: A Constraint-Oriented Runtime Middleware for Structure-Preserving Mapping under Non-Closure Conditions

detail.title: CausalPrime: A Constraint-Oriented Runtime Middleware for Structure-Preserving Mapping under Non-Closure Conditions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study is based exclusively on publicly available documents and runtime-generated structural observations. No human subjects, patient records, or personally identifiable information were involved. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and conventional semantic processing frameworks are typically optimized for continuity, probabilistic completion, and narrative coherence. Under ordinary interaction conditions, these mechanisms improve readability and stabilize downstream semantic interpretation. However, in high-responsibility environments characterized by incomplete, fragmented, or conflict-heavy input streams-such as forensic auditing, financial reconciliation, legal evidence tracing, and industrial telemetry inspection-continuity-driven optimization may suppress unresolved structural inconsistencies, missing dependencies, temporal discontinuities, and protocol conflicts that remain operationally critical for downstream inspection and replay validation. This paper presents CausalPrime, a constraint-oriented runtime middleware designed for structure-preserving observation under non-closure conditions. The system introduces the Minimal Causal Unit (MCU) as a typed intermediate representation (Typed IR) for localized state-transition registration under strict slot-negative constraints, together with runtime routing mechanisms including Relay propagation, Residual segregation, branch isolation, and explicit VOID registration. Rather than attempting to reconstruct objective truth or generate globally coherent semantic interpretations, the runtime registers what it can observe, routes unresolved structures into explicit failure states, and preserves those states without attempting semantic repair. A central design principle of the middleware is non-closure execution. Unresolved structures are treated as first-class runtime states rather than defects requiring probabilistic reconciliation or heuristic completion. Routing fractures, mutually exclusive branches, unresolved residuals, temporal order conflicts, and incomplete dependency chains remain explicitly observable within the runtime mapping matrix. The framework therefore prioritizes structural observability and replay-stable traceability over semantic completeness or narrative smoothness. To demonstrate the framework, the paper applies it to structured legal and audit document streams drawn from a real forensic case corpus (U.S. v. Kwok, 1:23-cr-00118-AT, Doc 834 [23]). Runtime stability is observed through a three-tier replay consistency framework across eight independent sessions spanning temperature 0.0 to 1.0. Preliminary replay observations indicate that the runtime preserves core structural routing patterns under the tested perturbation conditions, with backbone overlap ranging from 78-88% under neardeterministic extraction to 70-76% under maximum-entropy conditions. These results constitute case-study-level evidence within a single forensic document corpus; no statistical generalization is claimed. The execution boundary of the middleware is intentionally constrained. CausalPrime does not function as a theorem prover, world-modeling engine, causal truth inference framework, or autonomous reasoning system. Instead, it operates exclusively as a structurepreserving replay middleware for bounded runtime observation under incomplete inputs. Its primary engineering objective is to maintain replay-stable dependency traces, preserve observable failure states, and support traceable structural inspection workflows in environments where reliable closure cannot be guaranteed. This dual-layer constraint gap is discussed as an open design problem for constraint-oriented AI middleware in Section 7.5.1.

detail.abstract:
In the ceramics department of a university in Canada, students are required to wear respiratory protection when performing certain tasks involved in creating ceramic products as part of their coursework. This study aimed to assess exposure to respirable crystalline silica (RCS) during various ceramics production tasks and evaluate the necessity and suitability of the respirators currently used to mitigate this exposure.
An initial review of the SOP for ceramics production at the department, along with an assessment of the raw materials used and supporting literature, indicated that clay mixing, glaze mixing, unloading ceramics from kilns, and forming tasks in classrooms were activities likely to release RCS into the ambient air. Therefore, air samples were collected during these tasks, and respiratory protection was utilized throughout clay mixing and glaze mixing as required. A total of three area air samples were collected—one each during clay mixing, forming, and unloading tasks. Additionally, eight personal breathing zone air samples were taken, with four each during clay mixing and glaze mixing. 
The limited number of samples was due to challenges in scheduling glaze mixing and clay mixing tasks with technicians during a period of inconsistent ceramic work, compounded by tight project deadlines. The sampling procedure followed IRSST Method 206-2 for crystalline silica (quartz). The highest RCS concentration for personal breathing zone samples was 0.3 mg/m³ during clay mixing, which is 12 times the permissible exposure limit (PEL) of 0.025 mg/m³. This appears to be an outlier since the other RCS concentrations for personal breathing sample zones were 0.056, 0.021, 0.027, 0.1, 0.17; and two others below the Method Detection Limit (MDL). However, one personal breathing zone air sample during glaze mixing recorded 0.027 mg/m³, marginally exceeding the PEL by 0.002 mg/m³. 
In summary, 100% of personal breathing zone samples during clay mixing exceeded the PEL, while 25% of samples during glaze mixing also surpassed the PEL. This shows that clay mixing poses a significantly higher risk of RCS exposure to students involved in this task than glaze mixing in this department. Area air samples from both unloading kilns and forming showed RCS concentrations below the method detection limit. In contrast, the clay mixing room recorded an RCS concentration of 0.016 mg/m³, which is below the Permissible Exposure Limit (PEL) of 0.025 mg/m³. This indicates that ambient RCS levels in the clay mixing room are adequately controlled. However, the exceedance of the PEL highlights the increased risk of adverse health effects associated with high RCS exposure (from the source), including silicosis, lung cancer, and obstructive pulmonary disease.
To reduce these risks, students should continue wearing half-face masks with P100 filters during clay and glaze mixing as they are suitable to control these risks. Additionally, regularly consult professionals to maintain and test ventilation systems, especially in the clay mixing room, to ensure they operate at maximum efficiency. Also, continuously train and supervise students to position capture hoods correctly (to the source) and follow proper work practices to prevent dust dispersion during clay and glazing mixing. After implementing these controls, continue the existing air monitoring program to confirm that exposure levels remain effectively managed.

title: Cross-Border Payment Connectivity and the Portability Horizon: Does Digital-Government Maturity Travel?

detail.title: Cross-Border Payment Connectivity and the Portability Horizon: Does Digital-Government Maturity Travel?
detail.abstract: Whether two countries share a usable, monitored cross-border payment corridor is a question of digital-economy infrastructure, and policy increasingly assumes the answer follows from how digitally mature each country is at home. Governments and international organisations benchmark that domestic maturity with composite indices such as the World Bank GovTech Maturity Index (GTMI) and the UN E-Government Development Index (EGDI), and high scores are read as signals of broad digital readiness. We test that reading in international payments, combining the two indices with Remittance Prices Worldwide, the Global Findex, the Worldwide Governance Indicators, and the UN DESA bilateral migration matrix. Domestic maturity strongly predicts domestic financial inclusion, with r between 0.64 and 0.70. Its cross-border content is far weaker and conditional on income. In a gravity model of roughly 24,000 country pairs, maturity has no association with corridor existence on routes that involve a high-income economy and no robust association with corridor cost, so the pooled estimate is a near-zero (β =-0.13, p = 0.67). That pooled value is not a structural null. It averages opposing income-pairing regularities. Among South-South pairs, higher joint maturity is positively associated with corridor existence. The South-South result holds across both indices, which correlate at r = 0.82, and it survives a battery of robustness checks. It is also thin. It rests on roughly 60 to 70 monitored corridors, it is concentrated among a few regional hubs, and it does not extend to cost. Across every specification, connectivity is organised by bilateral migrant stock, shared language, and institutional proximity, which are properties of pairs of countries that no national benchmark records. We read this as an income-conditional portability horizon. A high national score is not a uniform signal of cross-border readiness, and national benchmarks should be paired with a dyadic measure of the readiness of two countries to interoperate, whose design and validation bar we specify.

title: Strategic Identity Asymmetry: Why Digital Infrastructure Governance Fails Where Technology Succeeds in Brazil, Nigeria, and the Philippines
affiliations: , University of Warwick and The Alan Turing Institute

detail.title: Strategic Identity Asymmetry: Why Digital Infrastructure Governance Fails Where Technology Succeeds in Brazil, Nigeria, and the Philippines
detail.abstract: Why do governments that invest heavily in digital identity infrastructure consistently fail to build the governance capacity needed for cross-border interoperability? Even technically mature, legally comprehensive systems cannot export trust in their credentials across borders. This paper investigates this puzzle through comparative institutional analysis of three middle-income regional anchors (Brazil, Nigeria, the Philippines) using the Standards-Aligned Assessment Framework for Interoperable Identity (SAAFII), a 96-indicator diagnostic instrument synthesizing thirteen international standards across eight socio-technical layers. Analysis reveals three institutional trajectories shaped by founding policy decisions: Brazil's 'Trust-First' path (PKI, 2001), Nigeria's 'Database-First' path (biometric enrollment, 2007), and the Philippines' 'Rights-First' path (privacy legislation, 2012). Despite divergent origins, all three converge on the same structural pattern: strong legal frameworks and operational technology coexist with persistent deficits in governance, accreditation, and assurance. We introduce Strategic Identity Asymmetry (SIA), a falsifiable mid-range institutional hypothesis predicting where technically mature digital infrastructure will fail institutionally. SIA explains this convergence through path-dependent lock-in and isomorphic mimicry, amplified by structural incentives favoring visible infrastructure investment over invisible governance capacity. Interoperability failure is an institutional governance problem, not a standards-compliance deficit. Key Points for Practitioners • Cross-border interoperability of digital identity credentials fails at governance and assurance layers, not at technology layers; reform priority should shift accordingly. • National governments should treat assurance framework development (IAL/AAL-equivalent tiers, accreditation schemes, trusted lists) as a prerequisite for, not a follow-up to, credential issuance at scale.

title: The Volatility Channel of the Deposit Franchise
affiliations: Prague University of Economics and Business

detail.title: The Volatility Channel of the Deposit Franchise

declarations.funderStatement: The research was supported by project IP100040 at the Prague University of Economics and Business.

detail.abstract: Deposit market power creates a volatility channel for bank profitability, distinct from the familiar level channel. Because banks reprice deposits asymmetrically, passing through rate increases more slowly than decreases, funding spreads are convex in the short rate, so expected net interest margins (NIM) depend on the volatility of the rate path, not only its level. This convexity is signed by the funding structure: positive for core-funded banks, negative for the rest, and positive on average. Using U.S. bank data from 1984-2025, we find realized short-rate volatility raises NIM, operating through funding costs and concentrating in discretionary deposit categories.

title: Cannabinoid Profiling of Cannabis sativa L. Samples from Different Regions of Nigeria Using Chromatographic Techniques
affiliations: Ahmadu Bello University, Ahmadu Bello University, Ahmadu Bello University,  and Ahmadu Bello University

detail.title: Cannabinoid Profiling of Cannabis sativa L. Samples from Different Regions of Nigeria Using Chromatographic Techniques
detail.abstract: Background: Cannabis sativa L. remains the most widely cultivated and consumed illicit drug in Nigeria, yet no comprehensive scientific data exists on the cannabinoid profiles of Nigerian-grown cannabis. With evolving global policies on cannabis and increasing calls for policy reform in Nigeria, establishing baseline chemical data on locally cultivated cannabis is imperative for forensic, medicinal, and regulatory purposes. Methods: Six cannabis samples were obtained through the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) from five geopolitical zones of Nigeria: Kaduna (North West; two samples are farm-cultivated and one sample is trafficker-confiscated), Adamawa (North East), Edo (South South), Enugu (South East), and Ondo (South West). Samples were extracted using acetonitrile/water (1:1 v/v). Cannabinoid analysis was performed using Thin Layer Chromatography (TLC) with hexane:ethyl acetate:acetic acid (4:1:0.1) mobile phase and High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) with UV detection at 240nm. Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (GC-MS) was employed for definitive compound identification and structural confirmation. Results: TLC analysis revealed 5-12 cannabinoid compounds per sample, with a total of 15 distinct cannabinoids identified across all samples. Samples from Ondo (F) and the trafficker-confiscated sample from Kaduna (A) each yielded 12 spots, while the Edo sample (D) produced 7 spots. Three compounds were common to all samples, with Rf values of 0.38, 0.57-0.58, and 0.61-0.63 (matching cannabidiol standard). HPLC analysis detected 15-25 compounds per sample, totalling 33 compounds across all samples, with 8 compounds common to all. Quantitative HPLC using cannabidiol as reference standard showed cannabinoid content ranging from 17.41 mg/g (Ondo) to 30.54 mg/g (Edo). GC-MS confirmed the presence of specific cannabinoids: Δ⁹-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabinol (CBN) in Samples A (trafficker-confiscated) and D (Edo); CBN only in Sample E (Enugu); and multiple cannabinoids—cannabidiol (CBD), cannabichromene (CBC), THC, and CBN in Sample F (Ondo). Notably, GC-MS failed to detect cannabinoids in Samples B (Kaduna farm) and C (Adamawa), suggesting limitations of the technique for samples with low cannabinoid concentrations. Conclusion: This first comprehensive cannabinoid profiling of Nigerian C. sativa reveals significant chemical heterogeneity among samples from different geographic regions. Each sample exhibited unique chromatographic fingerprints, demonstrating that chromatographic techniques can effectively distinguish cannabis of different origins. The Edo sample (D) showed the highest cannabinoid content, while the Ondo sample (F) displayed the most diverse cannabinoid profile. These findings have direct forensic applications for source attribution and provide essential baseline data for future medicinal cannabis research and evidence-based policy formulation in Nigeria.

title: Geopolitical Conditionality and the Transformation of Global Development Aid Priorities: Evidence from EU-Morocco Relations
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Geopolitical Conditionality and the Transformation of Global Development Aid Priorities: Evidence from EU-Morocco Relations
detail.abstract:
Global development aid has increasingly been shaped by donor geopolitical priorities rather than by poverty reduction or institutional reform objectives. This article introduces the concept of geopolitical conditionality to explain how strategic interests such as migration control, border security, and diplomatic alignment reshape aid allocation and implementation. The analysis draws on an original author-constructed dataset based on systematic coding of EU Multiannual Indicative Programs for Morocco covering the period 2007-2027 and is complemented by a comparison with Morocco and Tunisia over 2000-2024. 
The results indicate a clear shift in aid priorities toward security and migration, accompanied by implementation practices that favor short-term and measurable outputs over long-term institutional reforms. EU assistance generates tangible outputs, including infrastructure, renewable energy capacity, and border management improvements, but does not translate into sustained institutional change. 
The Moroccan case illustrates how large-scale and prolonged aid can fail to produce structural transformation when subordinated to geopolitical objectives. The contribution lies in specifying how geopolitical conditionality operates across the aid cycle by linking allocation decisions to implementation dynamics. The findings suggest that these mechanisms are not limited to EU-Morocco relations but are likely to arise in other contexts in which development aid becomes embedded in strategic exchange relationships. The scope conditions under which geopolitical conditionality constrains developmental outcomes are also identified.

title: Heterogeneous Impact of Teacher-Student Demographic Mismatch on Math and Science Achievement

detail.abstract: This paper focuses on the impact of teacher-student demographic mismatch on student success in 9th grade in U.S. high schools. In this paper, using data from the High School Longitudinal Survey of 2009 (HSLS:09), I investigate whether being assigned to a teacher of different sex and/or different race has significant negative impact on student achievement. HSLS:09 is the only nationally representative high school-level survey data that matches math and science teachers to students and student performance. I create a student-level short-panel dataset to find the effect of demographic mismatch in class on math and science class performance. The results show that having a different-sex teacher is disadvantageous for students of almost all racial backgrounds. Having a different-sex and different-race teacher is associated with achievement loss, especially for Black female students (0.3 standard deviations). Furthermore, the impact of demographic mismatch tends to be concentrated on Black students attending schools with less racial diversity.

title: Wage Dynamics of Foreign-Born Workers: Immigration Status, Mobility, and Policy
affiliations: University of Vermont

detail.title: Wage Dynamics of Foreign-Born Workers: Immigration Status, Mobility, and Policy
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the long-term wage differential between U.S. natives and foreign-born STEM graduates. Applying Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition on U.S. data from 2003 to 2021, I find that naturalized citizens and permanent residents earn more than U.S. natives, a gap not fully explained by predictors like job roles, education level, or STEM employment. Factors such as labor market laws, characteristics of foreign-born STEM workers, and limited visa availability significantly contribute to the `unexplained' wage gap between U.S. natives and foreign-born workers of two immigration statuses: naturalized citizens and permanent residents. This paper shows wage effects of changes in two factors on the persistence of the wage differentials, the requirement of employer sponsorship and the the restrictiveness of labor market entry - visa approval rate. I employ a worker-level pooled 2SLS model to demonstrate how changes in immigration status — specifically, naturalization and obtaining permanent residency — lead to an increase in wages for foreign-born STEM workers. This increase is likely due to the reduction in labor market barriers such as requirements of employer sponsorship that these workers face. Moreover, I analyze the causal effects of a significant policy change using a Difference-in-Differences (DID) model. Following the `Buy American and Hire American' executive order issued in 2017, there was an observed 11% wage increase for temporary workers in the U.S. STEM sector, likely resulting from a lower acceptance rate of worker H1B visa applications.

title: Regenerative Oman Tourism Accreditation Scheme: A Policy Note on Institutional Reform for Oman's Tourism Governance

detail.title: Regenerative Oman Tourism Accreditation Scheme: A Policy Note on Institutional Reform for Oman's Tourism Governance
detail.abstract: Oman's tourism sector lacks the institutional governance infrastructure to deliver on Vision 2040's sustainability ambitions. A tiered, modular Integrated Management System-the Regenerative Oman Tourism Accreditation Scheme (ROTAS)-provides a practical, scalable pathway from basic compliance to regenerative excellence. Effective delivery requires splitting the conventional DMO into two structurally independent bodies: a consultancy and capacity-building arm (ROCS) and an independent certification authority (ROTAS). A proof of concept exists: a small Omani marine tourism operator in Qantab implemented an early version of this model, securing three major resort contracts and recognition at the Al Roya Economic Prize special mention within two years. The Ministry of Heritage and Tourism has previously expressed interest in this initiative. This note calls for the formalisation of that dialogue and the launch of a national pilot programme.

title: Managing Innovation and Technology in Developing Countries
affiliations: Lawrence Technological University

detail.title: Managing Innovation and Technology in Developing Countries
detail.abstract: Innovation and technology management is an inevitable issue in the high end technological and innovative organizations. Today, most of the innovations are limited with developed countries like USA, Japan and Europe while developing countries are still behind in the field of innovation and management of technology. But it is also becoming a subject for rapid progress and development in developing countries. Innovation and technology environment in developing countries are by nature, problematic, characterized by ordinary business models, political instability and governance conditions, low education level and lack of world-class research universities, an underdeveloped and mediocre physical infrastructure, and lack of solid technology based on trained human resources. This paper provides a theoretical and conceptual framework analysis for managing innovation and technology in developing countries like India and China. We present the issues and challenges in innovation and technology management and come up with proposed solutions.

title: Platform-Driven Hate Speech: An Epidemiological Model with Optimal Taxation
affiliations: Universitas Mercatorum

detail.title: Platform-Driven Hate Speech: An Epidemiological Model with Optimal Taxation
detail.abstract: Online hate speech is a global challenge amplified by engagement-driven social media algorithms. This paper develops an epidemiological model of hate speech propagation capturing the strategic interaction between a profit-maximizing platform and a welfare-maximizing government. The platform's profit depends on the prevalence of hate speech and on its own algorithmic reactivity, creating a feedback loop between the epidemic and economic incentives. The government sets an optimal tax on amplification to internalize the social costs, balancing the benefit of tax revenue against the deadweight loss of taxation. The Stackelberg equilibrium is characterised analytically and solved numerically. The optimal tax reduces hate speech prevalence, eliminates bistability, and lowers victim harm.

title: Armed Conflict and Solidarity Voting: Evidence from the Eurovision Song Contest
affiliations: Université Panthéon-Assas (Paris II)

detail.title: Armed Conflict and Solidarity Voting: Evidence from the Eurovision Song Contest
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether countries involved in armed conflict receive systematically more points at the Eurovision Song Contest (ESC), and whether any such solidarity effect is driven by popular sentiment or by institutional signaling. Using a dyadic panel covering all ESC grand finals from 1957 to 2025, we estimate difference-indifferences models exploiting conflict onset as a source of quasi-experimental variation. Our main finding is striking : conflict-affected countries receive no additional points from professional juries, but are awarded approximately 6 additional points by the public televote, an effect significant at the 1% level. Event study estimates for Ukraine and Israel confirm that this solidarity bonus emerges sharply at conflict onset and does not pre-exist it. These results support a popular empathy mechanism and reject the institutional signaling hypothesis, suggesting that geopolitical shocks propagate into cultural arenas in ways that reflect public opinion more than diplomatic positioning.

title: Continuous-Time Sequence-Space Jacobians: Large-Scale Dynamics and Risk
affiliations: University of Hamburg

detail.title: Continuous-Time Sequence-Space Jacobians: Large-Scale Dynamics and Risk
detail.abstract: Sequence-space methods solve heterogeneous-agent transition dynamics by mapping paths of aggregate shocks into paths of aggregate outcomes. Auclert et al. (2025a) show stationary Jacobians are quasi-Toeplitz, enabling existence and uniqueness diagnostics, truncation control, and large-T , large-N solution without dense matrix algebra. We develop the continuoustime counterpart. Stationary responses become convolutions in relative time, while the datezero experiment generates a compact missing-anticipation correction. This structure gives continuous-time fake-news densities, real-line frequency diagnostics for equilibrium index balance, and inverse-symbol regularizers for matrix-free computation. We derive the structure for stationary heterogeneous-agent blocks and apply it to the 22-sector HANK-IO model of Schaab and Tan (2023). We further provide a continuous-time route to second-order risk. Itô's lemma identifies covariance-weighted curvature as a local source in HJBs, pricing equations, and equilibrium residuals. We turn these terms into sequence-space right-hand sides and propagate anticipated risk, size dependence, and state dependence with the first-order inverse.

title: Building a Future-Ready Workforce: Policy Memo

detail.title: Building a Future-Ready Workforce: Policy Memo

detail.abstract: India has a comprehensive framework for skill development with centrally sponsored schemes and PPP models. Despite improvements in the rate of overall unemployment, significant gaps and challenges still exist. Numerous reports by international agencies like ILO, and the World Economic Forum suggest that due to the changing landscape of the future of work, increased automation, and digitalization, there is a need for reskilling unemployed youth and upskilling the current workforce in emerging fields such as AI, robotics, and renewable energy. AI-enabled skill development programs focus on both tech and non-tech workforce development along with soft skills development. To address the unemployment problem, placement-linked support is provided with blockchain-verified digital certificates and skill badges. To address the diversity of the workforce and regional disparities in India, financial aid, support services, and outreach plans along with high-tech industrial collaboration will be put in place. Considering the impact of automation on traditional industries, economic transition support for automation-displaced workers is provided. The most important element of the skill development model is the sustainability framework to ensure the programs are self-sustaining financial models.

title: FoodLink AI: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Platforms for Reducing Food Waste through Food Redistribution

detail.title: FoodLink AI: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Platforms for Reducing Food Waste through Food Redistribution
detail.abstract: This assignment examines the issue of food waste and the use of new technologies for reducing it. The paper focuses on FoodLink AI, a proposed digital platform that uses artificial intelligence to connect businesses with food banks, charities, volunteers and platform administrators. Food waste is analyzed as a social, economic and environmental problem, with emphasis on causes across the food supply chain, such as weak demand forecasting, storage problems, overproduction and poor coordination. The assignment explains how the platform records food donations, how the AI decides which organization should receive each donation, how delivery is confirmed and what reports the system produces. The aim is to present a specific and practical technology-based solution for food redistribution.

detail.abstract: Climate change disproportionately affects vulnerable communities despite their relatively low contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions. This imbalance has led to increasing attention toward climate justice, which emphasizes fairness, equity, and the protection of communities most affected by environmental change. This study examines the relationship between climate justice and local communities, focusing on community experiences, adaptation strategies, and perceptions of environmental equity. Using a mixed-methods descriptive research design, data were collected through surveys, interviews, focus group discussions, and document analysis. Findings reveal that local communities experience significant climate-related challenges, including extreme weather events, livelihood disruptions, and environmental degradation. The study further highlights the importance of community participation, inclusive policymaking, and equitable resource allocation in promoting climate resilience. The study concludes that climate justice is essential in addressing environmental inequalities and ensuring sustainable development among vulnerable communities.

title: Generative AI Art and Copyright Governance: Rethinking the Adaptation Right and its Limits

detail.title: Generative AI Art and Copyright Governance: Rethinking the Adaptation Right and its Limits
detail.abstract:
Generative AI has become part of contemporary artistic practice, enabling the creation of texts, images, music, and audiovisual works through processes of variation, recombination, and transformation. As AI-generated outputs increasingly resemble existing works, disputes have intensified over how such creative connections should be understood and governed. Much of the current copyright debate approaches these questions through the lens of reproduction, focusing on copying during AI training or in the process of generating outputs. This emphasis leaves an important gap: how to evaluate creative reliance that is non-literal, indirect, and difficult to trace to specific technical processes.

This article addresses that gap by revisiting the copyright framework governing adaptations and derivative works. Rather than treating copyright doctrine as a fixed set of rules, the analysis approaches it as an evolving conceptual framework shaped by changing modes of cultural production. By examining the historical development of the adaptation right, its implementation across jurisdictions, and its relationship to the principle that copyright protects expression rather than ideas, the article highlights its potential to govern forms of creative transformation that fall between copying and independent creation.

Building on this insight, the article proposes an output-oriented inquiry based on “substantial recognisable linkage,” asking whether an AI-generated work can reasonably be perceived as drawing on protectable expression in a prior work, rather than merely reflecting shared styles, genres, or ideas. Focusing on the observable qualities of AI-generated outputs as they are perceived in their cultural context, this approach offers a conceptual vocabulary aligned with creative practices such as remix, variation, and stylistic exploration. At the same time, the article emphasises that any broader reliance on adaptation-based protection must be accompanied by robust exceptions and limitations, in order to preserve artistic experimentation, cultural exchange, and freedom of expression in AI-mediated creative environments.

title: Machine Learning, Real-time Macroeconomic Risk, and Asset Pricing
affiliations: University of Ottawa - Telfer School of Management and

detail.title: Machine Learning, Real-time Macroeconomic Risk, and Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: We develop a framework for measuring and pricing macroeconomic risk in real time by integrating high-frequency textual information into a structural long-run risk asset-pricing model. Using daily news articles processed through Fine-Grained Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (Fi-GAS), we construct a sentiment-augmented macroeconomic measure that classifies the economy into distinct business-cycle states and captures evolving economic conditions at high frequency. The results show that bad states are characterized by lower expected consumption growth, elevated macroeconomic uncertainty, and higher long-run risk premia, while good states exhibit stronger growth and lower compensation for risk. Applying the model to a broad cross-section of publicly traded U.S. firms, we find that the sentiment-augmented long-run risk factor closely tracks observed excess returns and captures substantial cross-sectional heterogeneity in firm-level risk premia and return volatility. Overall, the findings suggest that real-time textual information contains economically meaningful signals about persistent macroeconomic risk and materially improves the empirical performance of structural asset-pricing models.

title: Generalized Physically-Consistent Kernel Density Estimation with Limited Grouped Data Contamination

detail.title: Generalized Physically-Consistent Kernel Density Estimation with Limited Grouped Data Contamination

keywords: Fredholm Integral Equation of the Second Kind

detail.abstract: This paper treats the deconvolution model Y = SX1 + (1-S) k j=1 Xj where k is a known integer satisfying k ≥ 2, S has a known Bernoulli distribution with P [S = 1] ∈ (0, 1), and (X1, ..., X k) are I.I.D. from a distribution having Lebesgue density fX. The aim is to estimate fX using observations from Y. A prominent application arises in finance, where high-frequency asset returns do not always exclusively reflect current news due to information lags. Unlike the classic grouped data deconvolution model where P [S = 1] = 0 (Meister 2007), this estimation problem is well-posed provided P [S = 1] is large enough. This substantially reduces the difficulty of the estimation problem. The proposed estimator has a Mean Integrated Square Error (MISE) converging at a rate which is equal to the optimal nonparametric rate of Fan (1993) without data grouping (i.e. if P [S = 1] = 1). Moreover, if the distribution of S is unknown, then a feasible estimator is proposed if the first moment of X is known or else if Xj represents the lag of order j-1 for some stationary process. The feasible estimator has an Integrated Square Error (ISE) which enjoys the same rate of convergence in probability. The methodology is easy to implement from data using a single tuning parameter. A Monte Carlo experiment reveals good finite-sample properties for the proposed estimator.

detail.abstract: The worth of a state, in the long run, is the worth of the individuals composing it." ~ John Stuart Mill, The Philosopher. In this scholarly examination, This scholarly discourse endeavours to dissect the multifaceted panorama of India's democratic institutions and electoral mechanisms, traversing four cardinal themes: the historical medley that contextualizes the subcontinent's parliamentary democracy, the labyrinthine intricacies of its electoral framework, the persistent conundrums engendered by internal migratory flows vis-à-vis electoral engagement, and the prospective corridors for reformative strides in the electoral domain. The historical vista delineates the genesis of India's parliamentary edifice, a construct influenced by the Westminster model, amalgamated with the indigenous politico-administrative ethos. The constitutional bulwark fortifies individual liberties and minority safeguards, concurrently instituting affirmative stratagems to redress historical inequities. Notwithstanding these provisions, the herculean task of harmonizing the nation's ethnic, linguistic, and religious heterogeneity, preserving the sanctity of autonomous institutions, and extirpating the hydra of corruption persists as a Sisyphean endeavour. Recent studies indicate declining democratic health worldwide, with worrying signs of increasing attacks on journalists, targeted harassment of activists, and diminished judicial independence in India. Active citizens play vital roles in sustaining and reinforcing democratic principles, participating in policymaking, monitoring abuse of power, and demanding transparency and accountability. To invigorate the sinews of Indian democracy, a multipronged strategy is imperative, encompassing the fortification of institutional frameworks, the staunch defence of minority entitlements, the proliferation of civic pedagogy, the elevation of subaltern narratives, the dismantlement of participatory impediments, and the astute harnessing of technological advancements. The variegated democracy indices serve as a prism reflecting the intricate interplay between localized political dynamics and overarching macroeconomic vectors that sculpt the governance landscape. The heterogeneity of these indices accentuates the imperative for a holistic and nuanced approach to appraising the trajectory of democratic norms, cognizant of the labyrinthine task of quantifying democratic maturation or regression.

title: Modular Default Rules. Rereading Hadley v. Baxendale and the Theory of Contractual Defaults

detail.title: Modular Default Rules. Rereading Hadley v. Baxendale and the Theory of Contractual Defaults
detail.abstract:
In the economic theory of contract, the rule of Hadley v. Baxendale is usually described as a default rule that excludes the recoverability of consequential damages and, in particular, as the paradigmatic example of a penalty default rule. On this reading, by excluding the recoverability of consequential damages, the rule requires promisees who seek broader coverage to contract around the default through a different contractual term. The rule is unwelcome to the majority of promisees, who would prefer a rule of full liability. This Article argues that this account fails to capture the rule’s actual structure. Hadley is not a rule that excludes consequential damages, but a default rule internally articulated into two modules: an ordinary module, which covers the losses arising naturally from the breach in the ordinary course of events, and an extended module, which covers special damages when the promisor had been informed of them, or had reason to know of the circumstances that made them foreseeable.

The rereading of Hadley yields a theoretical consequence of general character. It makes it possible to isolate a new type of default rule, here termed the “modular default rule.” By modular default rule is meant a rule that contains within itself several operative modules. The standard module governs the ordinary case and operates without any action by the parties. The extended module is triggered when one party makes knowable private circumstances capable of justifying a different liability regime. Communication is the condition that allows the default itself to extend its effects.

detail.abstract: Why do some digital products charge users directly (2C), while others rely on businessside monetization (2B)? Existing two-sided market and media economics literatures treat user heterogeneity as exogenous and assume 2C pricing is always feasible, focusing on "how to price" conditional on a given product architecture. They do not explain whether unified 2C pricing is structurally possible at all, nor why some product architectures systematically preclude it. This paper shifts the question from optimal pricing to contractual feasibility. Building on transaction cost theory, we argue that product architecture determines whether a firm can draw a coherent target customer persona. When a product bundles highly heterogeneous use cases (e.g., a superapp, a generalpurpose AI model), no single persona fits; unified 2C pricing becomes infeasible because the firm cannot effectively separate consumers by their willingness to pay at acceptable cost. Monetization then shifts to 2B channels or layered contracts. To isolate this mechanism, we employ an extreme-case design with within-firm comparisons (Tencent WeChat vs. its gaming and music units) and longitudinal changes (The New York Times before and after divestiture). Cross-industry evidence from media, platforms, software, and AI confirms that narrower, coherent products support 2C pricing, whereas broader, heterogeneous systems necessitate 2B models. This paper contributes by endogenizing user heterogeneity to observable product structure, moving beyond the abstract parameters of existing models. Furthermore, it extends the logic of audience clarity-originally confined to media economics-to digital platforms, open-source software, and generative AI, demonstrating that functional heterogeneity imposes similar structural.
